label: JAL 123, a Boeing 747SR bound for Osaka, is cleared for take-off from Haneda runway 15L. 509 passengers and 15 crew are aboard on the eve of the Obon holiday.
Lift-off. The first officer flies from the left seat as part of his captain training; the captain, his instructor, sits on the right.
Gear up (not recorded; estimated, 9 s after lift-off)
Tokyo Control clears the flight direct to the Seaperch waypoint. The climb to 24,000 ft continues over Sagami Bay.
Most of the fin, the rudders and the tail cone lost
A loud bang at 23,900 ft. The aft pressure bulkhead, weakened by an improper repair after a 1978 tail strike, bursts. Cabin air rushes into the tail.
The blast tears away most of the vertical fin and the rudder and severs all four hydraulic systems. The crew sets the emergency code 7700.
The captain reports trouble to Tokyo Control and asks to return to Haneda.
The aircraft begins to oscillate: a slow climb-and-sink cycle of about 90 seconds (phugoid) and a rolling, yawing sway every 11 seconds (Dutch roll).
The flight engineer confirms all hydraulic pressure is lost. From now on the crew can steer only by changing the thrust of the engines.
Tokyo Control offers Nagoya, 72 miles away; the captain asks for Haneda instead. To make it easier for the crew, the controller switches to Japanese.
The flight engineer learns that the ceiling at the rear of the cabin has collapsed, and suggests an emergency descent.
He tells JAL's company radio that a rear door, R5, has broken and that they are descending. No one yet knows the real cause.
The aircraft passes north of Mount Fuji and turns east toward Tokyo, still climbing and sinking every minute or so.
The crew tries to lower the landing gear to steady the aircraft. It will not come down: the normal system needs hydraulic pressure.
The flight engineer lowers the gear with the alternate system, letting it fall under its own weight. The extra drag damps the pitching.
Over Otsuki the aircraft circles to the right, a full turn and more, descending from about 22,000 to 17,000 ft. Uneven engine thrust is turning it.
Down to 13,500 ft, the aircraft turns northeast toward the Okutama mountains. The captain radios again that it is uncontrollable.
“Can you control the aircraft now?” “It's uncontrollable.”
Mountains ahead. The captain calls for a right turn and maximum power to climb away from them.
Full power stops the descent low over the Okutama mountains, but the nose now pitches steeply up.
The nose rises to almost 40° and the speed falls to 108 knots: the aircraft stalls. The stall warning sounds; maximum power recovers it.
The captain and the flight engineer agree to control the pitch with engine power alone.
Flaps start to extend on alternate power
To gain some control, the flaps are lowered with the slow alternate electric system. They will take minutes to move.
The captain reports a third time that the aircraft is uncontrollable. It has climbed back to about 13,000 ft, heading west-northwest into the mountains of Gunma.
Tokyo Approach gives their position: 55 miles northwest of Haneda, 25 miles west of Kumagaya. Haneda and the Yokota air base are both ready to receive them.
Flaps about 25; retraction begins at once
As the flaps reach about 25 units, the aircraft rolls steeply to the right and the nose drops. The crew retracts the flaps and adds power.
The aircraft dives at more than 18,000 ft per minute, 36° nose down and banked 70° to the right. The ground proximity warning sounds.
